extracted.intended_audience: IGCSE (Cambridge CIE) English Language students preparing Paper 2 Section B narrative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and an exam-focused rubric for producing high-mark narrative/composition answers for Cambridge IGCSE English Language Paper 2 Section B. Covers planning, structure (Freytag's Pyramid), characterisation, setting, linguistic devices and exam technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a specific purpose and form; adapt tone, style and register
rubrics_metrics.description: Section B requires you to write for a specific purpose and in a specific form. To get the highest mark you will need to adapt your tone, style and register for different forms, purposes and audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone: the sound of the narrator’s 'voice' should be appropriate and convincing. Register: vocabulary and phrasing should suit the purpose. Style: sentence structure and overall structure should be dynamic and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan before writing (10–15 minutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: As with any extended piece of writing, planning is vital. You should spend 10-15 minutes mind-mapping your ideas before you start writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mind-map or representation of Freytag’s Pyramid to plot out your story; plan characters, perspective, and reminders of figurative language to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop an idea to a conclusion; plan an ending with a resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative story writing develops an idea to a conclusion. In the exam, it is best to plan an ending with a resolution (decide whether it ends happily or not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abrupt endings or no ending at all. You may choose a resolved ending or a suspenseful cliff-hanger (not a sudden or clichéd ending).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep plot simple: one main event, limited characters and settings
rubrics_metrics.description: In the exam, it is best not to plan a complex story over a long period, with multiple characters, settings or plot twists. Plan one main event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your plot is simple enough to be coherent and cohesive; stick to no more than two characters and one main setting to maintain control in limited time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structural techniques (e.g., flashback) correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider employing structural techniques, such as a flashback, to give background information and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a flashback, ensure you use past-tense verbs for this and make it clear to the reader how the flashback relates to the main event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop characters and consider archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider essential narrative character archetypes, such as 'villain', 'victim', 'hero', etc., and decide how your characters fit these descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should represent ideas (hope, strength, abandonment) or roles (injustice, evil). Well-rounded characters should be taken on a journey and undergo development or change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe people focusing on relevant details only
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing people, focus on relevant details only (for example, the important colours or physical details that matter to the story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid irrelevant detail; include facial expressions or single vivid details (e.g., 'her tear-stained face') where they add meaning or characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal character through movement, body language and verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use movements and body language as an effective way to describe characters and convey emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verbs and adverbs (power verbs) and actions (e.g., 'his head dropped') to show rather than tell; choose alternative verbs to 'said' (e.g., 'whispered', 'bellowed').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue and dialogue verbs to reveal character (sparingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: If using dialogue, the verbs you use to describe how characters speak can reveal more about them than the words themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit dialogue, especially if unsure about punctuation. Use speech marks and punctuation accurately. Ensure dialogue progresses characterisation or plot rather than being filler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition and motif for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: It is effective to repeat ideas related to colour or repeat ideas for emphasis; use repetition as a motif.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition works best when planned as a motif repeated throughout the piece to reinforce theme or mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure responses into five or six paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative writing responses should be structured into five or six paragraphs. Plan your response carefully given the time limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A five-part structure (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution) helps control and pace the story; paragraph lengths may vary for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition: establish setting, perspective, characters and hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition (setting the scene) — stick to one main setting and start at the location. Hook your reader and give clues about what will happen later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide narrative perspective and tense (first person and past tense are easier to control). Introduce no more than two characters. Employ the five senses and ensure the scene's mood reflects the main character's mood. This paragraph could end with an inciting incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rising action: build tension and develop character
rubrics_metrics.description: The rising action paragraph should build tension, drama or interest and directly lead to the turning point (climax).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop characters using dialogue, monologue, direct or indirect characterisation to create three-dimensional characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax: provide the turning point and change
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax is the turning point where everything changes and characters cannot go back. The protagonist may face an external problem or an internal choice/dilemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protagonist's choice should be made in this paragraph. Vary sentence structure, length and language here for dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falling action: show consequences and internal response
rubrics_metrics.description: The falling action should result directly from the climax and show the consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on characters' thoughts and feelings as a result of the climax to continue developing characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution/denouement: resolve or cliff-hanger; avoid clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose to resolve your story, or end on a cliff-hanger (not a sudden ending). Avoid clichés such as 'I woke up and it was all a dream.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reflecting a change in setting/atmosphere from the opening, or referring back to earlier imagery to create a cyclical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary paragraph length for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph lengths should not all be the same; better answers vary paragraph lengths for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What matters is developing separate ideas or points in each paragraph and avoiding repetitive descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build setting with sensory language and consistent mood
rubrics_metrics.description: The setting should reflect your main character’s mood (pathetic fallacy) and be built using sensory language (five senses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe dark/light, colours, sounds, smells and weather. Allow a paragraph to describe scene without confusing readers with who is there. Ensure all descriptive language builds the same mood and avoid mixing incompatible images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrasting scenes to convey change and engage reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasting scenes is an effective way to convey ideas and engage the reader (e.g., sunny afternoon turning to storm as mood changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make contrasts reflect the character’s mood and the story progression; don't give too much away at once — keep the reader guessing with controlled reveals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer indirect characterisation (show) over direct (tell)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect characterisation (showing through speech, thoughts, actions and others' views) creates more complex, well-rounded characters; direct characterisation (telling) can make characters superficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indirect methods (monologue, actions, dialogue) to build relatable characters; use direct characterisation sparingly for broad details where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use monologue and first-person voice to create intimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use first-person, a monologue helps readers engage with the character and creates a personal tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a character's 'voice' using punctuation, short sentences or questions to indicate emotions (e.g., nervousness). Use emotive language to help readers understand the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make deliberate linguistic choices; consider connotations and 'show, not tell'
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing language and techniques, make deliberate choices for effect and consider word connotations. Employ the principle of 'show, not tell'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use words that evoke emotions or reveal character background. Plan figurative language to add depth rather than using it gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use literary/linguistic devices appropriately (list and tips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ devices such as repetition, alliteration, metaphor, personification, onomatopoeia, simile, imagery, juxtaposition, emotive language, power verbs and pathetic fallacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition: use as a motif. Alliteration: use for effect (not necessarily adjacent words). Metaphor: can be simple or extended. Personification: good for atmosphere. Onomatopoeia: be sophisticated and avoid ALL CAPS. Simile: use sparingly. Imagery: engage senses. Juxtaposition: place contrasts side-by-side. Emotive language: evoke strong response. Power verbs: choose deliberate action verbs to create picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing or contradictory descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure descriptive language is coherent (e.g., do not mix contradictory sensory details that confuse the reader).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example warning: 'The graveyard was dark, cold and smelled like fragrant flowers' is confusing — keep images consistent with intended mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam technique checklist (Steps to success)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow practical steps: read the two task options carefully, highlight the one you have a strong idea for, plan, write, and leave time to proofread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend 10-15 minutes planning (mind-map or Freytag’s Pyramid), plan characters and perspective, note figurative techniques to include, write the story sticking to your plan, and try to leave five minutes at the end to re-read and correct obvious mistakes.
